content.title: About
content.content: Soup made with pork or ham is a traditional dish prepared from a meat broth, pieces of pork or ham, vegetables and spices. It has a rich flavor, aromatic profile and a warming effect, often served in colder seasons.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork soups are popular in Eastern European, Asian and Latin American cuisines.
Ham adds a smoky note that intensifies with long simmering.
The classic Russian rassolnik is often made on a pork broth with salted cucumbers.
Japan’s “tonkatsu ramen” includes a fried pork cutlet in the broth.
Using bones in pork soup increases gelatin content, making the broth thicker.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Pork and ham provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Pork contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The soup supplies thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Calcium, phosphorus and zinc from bones and meat support bone health and the immune system.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A warm broth helps maintain fluid balance, especially in cold weather.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soups are often salted; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Ham and fatty pork cuts contain saturated fats, which should be limited in heart disease.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have allergic reactions to pork proteins.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Insufficiently boiled broth may harbor pathogens; ensure it reaches a rolling boil.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, often with noodles, rice, potatoes or fresh vegetables. Garnish with herbs, sour cream or a dash of hot sauce to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the soup to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 2 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before consuming.
